lesson.title: Data first
lesson.subtitle: Plan it, collect it, check it

video.title: Data first
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — your computer studies teacher, Kenya (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: A model that got it wrong

scenes.visual: The school garden after class. Mr Joseph kneels by a bean plant with a phone, a few students around him. On the phone screen, a photo of a leaf with brown spots, and the model’s answer underneath: a green ‘healthy’ tag. He photographs a second spotted leaf: ‘healthy’ again. He looks up, puzzled, then half-smiles.
scenes.animation: Phone screen slides up; the ‘healthy’ tag pops in twice (≤ 200 ms each). Quick push-in on Joseph’s face.
scenes.narration: Last term, my class trained a model to spot sick bean leaves. It called almost every leaf healthy, even the sick ones! The computer wasn’t the problem. Our data was.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the course name, the lesson title and a yellow ‘AI’ track chip with the spark icon.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: data first, because a model can only learn what its examples show it.

scenes.visual: A wordless model box sits alone on a plain background, with no window onto the garden. Leaf photos slide towards it one at a time, each with a tag clipped on: a check (healthy) or a warning triangle (sick). The tagged photos stack into a pile labelled with a database icon.
scenes.animation: Photos slide in on a curve; tags clip on (150 ms each); the pile grows.
scenes.on_screen_text: Your data is all it knows
scenes.narration: A model never sees the garden. All it knows comes from your examples. Each one is something you collected, like a leaf photo, plus a label: the right answer, “healthy” or “sick”. Together, they’re your data.

scenes.visual: A student’s notebook page titled ‘Data plan’ fills in line by line: what to collect (a leaf sketch), the labels (two tags), how many (a tally of ten and ten), how varied (small sketches: a young leaf, an old leaf, a sun, a cloud, two different phones).
scenes.animation: Each line writes itself in as it is said (≤ 300 ms); tally marks tick in.
scenes.narration: So plan before you collect anything. What will you collect: photos of bean leaves? Which labels: healthy and sick? How many: at least ten of each, to start? And how varied: young and old leaves, sun and shade, different phones?

scenes.visual: Three problem cards drop onto a table. First: a spotted leaf wearing a ‘healthy’ tag, circled in red. Second: a tiny pile of five photos beside an empty space. Third: a seesaw with ninety leaf icons on one side and ten on the other, tipped hard.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in one by one (150 ms bounce); the red circle draws; the seesaw tips.
scenes.narration: Then check for three problems. Wrong labels: a sick leaf filed as healthy teaches a wrong answer. Too few examples: five photos can’t show every way a leaf looks. And one kind far outnumbering another: ninety healthy leaves and ten sick, like Mr Joseph’s class.

scenes.visual: Clean white card with the AI track chip. The word ‘dataset’ appears, then three badges build under it: a check-square (correct labels), a stack of boxes (enough of each kind), layered cards in different colours (a fair mix).
scenes.animation: Badges pop in left to right, 300 ms apart.
scenes.narration: A dataset is all the labelled examples a model learns from. A good one has correct labels, enough of each kind, and a fair mix of everything it will meet.

scenes.visual: A single school textbook on a desk, with the model box sitting behind it like a student revising. The book flips open to the answers page: two answers are crossed in red. It flips to the contents: ‘Fractions: page 1 of 1’, and the model box looks worried.
scenes.animation: Page flips (300 ms); red crosses draw; the contents line highlights.
scenes.narration: Think of your data as the model’s only textbook. If answers in the back are wrong, it learns wrong answers. If there’s one page on fractions, it won’t be ready for fractions in the exam.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma pops in beside a grid of tomato photos, all lit by the same harsh noon sun, one eyebrow raised. Three answer cards drop in below her.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Your class photographs forty ripe and forty unripe tomatoes, all at noon in bright sun. What’s missing?

scenes.visual: The card ‘Photos in other light’ gets a blue check badge. Split screen: on the left, the noon photos, all bright; on the right, the same tomatoes at dawn, in shade, and under a market umbrella at dusk, where the model box shows a question mark.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms). The right side fades from bright to dim in 1 s.
scenes.narration: Photos in other light. The model never saw shade, dusk or a dim market stall. It may fail the first time it meets one. Eighty is a good start, but variety matters as much as numbers.

scenes.visual: Three quick cards, about 5 seconds each: a student holding a phone out to a classmate, who nods before speaking into it; a page of handwriting that reads as wavy lines, with no name at the top; a market stall photographed from above, fruit in frame, the seller out of shot.
scenes.animation: Each card flips in from the side. A small ‘hand’ icon pops on each when permission is shown.
scenes.narration: Collect fairly, too. Recording voices? Ask each person first, and say what it’s for. Photographing handwriting? Use a made-up sentence, never names or addresses. Taking photos at the market? Photograph the fruit, not the sellers, unless they agree.

scenes.visual: A phone screen showing the ‘Teach it to see’ lab: a small drawing grid, buttons to add a drawing as a circle, a cross or a line, and three rows of example thumbnails. A finger draws a circle, adds it, presses Train; bars show what the network thinks of a new drawing.
scenes.animation: The circle draws itself on the grid (1 s); the thumbnail drops into its row; the bars fill left to right.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: teach it to see
scenes.narration: In the app, you’ll teach a small network to see. Draw a circle, a cross or a line, and add it to its group. Press Train, then test a new drawing. Then remove examples, or add a messy one, and see what changes.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph holds up a pile of exercise books from the class. Three answer cards appear beside him.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. You want to train a model on your classmates’ handwriting. What should you do first?

scenes.visual: The ‘Ask each one’ card gets the check badge, then the screen resolves into four summary lines and a closing line.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in one by one, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Ask each one first, and keep names off the pages. Remember: plan what to collect, the labels, how many and how varied. Check for wrong labels, too few examples and one kind outnumbering another. A model is only as good as its data.

scenes.visual: A student at a market stall with a notebook, sorting tomatoes into two piles and ticking a tally; at home, the same student lays leaves out on a table and photographs them. Mr Joseph gives a thumbs up. End card: the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Tally marks tick in; the piles grow. End card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: collect twenty labelled examples of something around you: leaves, fruit at the market, or handwriting. Count each label. Then write down what’s missing: other kinds, other light, other places.

checkpoints.prompt: Forty ripe and forty unripe tomatoes, all photographed at noon in bright sun. What’s missing?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — without shade, dusk or a dim market stall in the data, the model may fail the first time it meets them.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — eighty is a good start, but every photo has the same light. The model needs variety: shade, morning, evening.

checkpoints.prompt: You want to train a model on your classmates’ handwriting. What should you do first?

options.text: Use old pages they threw away
Ask the teacher, not the classmates
Ask each one, and leave names off

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — it’s their handwriting, so they decide. Ask each person, say what it’s for, and keep names off the pages.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — thrown-away pages and a teacher’s yes don’t replace asking each classmate. Ask first, and keep names off.
